doc.title: Art Farmer — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Violin teacher Mr. Reynolds and jazz as the devil's music
summary: His violin teacher, and the stigma in the black community that jazz was the devil's music, which made the jam sessions exciting.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Do you remember any of the names of the teachers you had, your piano teacher or any other music teachers?

I remember the name of the man that I used to take violin lessons from. I know his name was Mr. Reynolds. He said when you hold the violin, you have the hold your left hand like you’re clutching your pear from the tree [laughs]. That’s gonna stay with me forever. I thought that was very poetic. But like I said, there was a certain stigma to playing music, playing jazz. Some people say that’s the devil’s music.
You actually heard people tell you this coming up?
Yeah, they’d say that’s the devil’s music.
So, there was some biased against it?
Yeah, in the black community, that was the devil’s music. You could only play music to praising God, for the praise of God in the church.
Like any precocious youngster, that probably inspired you to want to play it [laughs]. Do you remember when you first, well, you said you heard the jam session, heard the band playing…
Yeah, I heard the kids jamming, I said, that’s great.
That’s what turned it around for you. You knew what type of music you wanted to play at that point.
